claim.why_it_matters: Sibling clauses at the same numeric depth are transcribed at different markdown heading levels, so the derived outline mis-parents them: D.11.2/.3/.4 render as peers of D.11 rather than children of it, and D.13.3.2/.3/.4 as peers of D.13.3 rather than children. Anything that reconstructs clause structure from heading level - a generated table of contents, anchor/citation depth, a section-scoped search over the spec - reads the annex hierarchy wrongly, and D.12.1 'General' in particular becomes indistinguishable in level from the clause D.12 it belongs to. The pattern across the file is that only the FIRST subclause under a parent keeps its correct level and every later sibling is promoted to '##'; the adjacent batch (compare-p1114-p1125.json) reported the identical defect for D.14.3.2.3 onward.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on three independent grounds after rendering PDF p1103 (printed folio 1073) and p1102 (folio 1072) at 300 dpi and reading both against specs/ISO_COBOL.md. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING - the claimed kind is simply wrong. Page 1103 prints exactly two headings, 'D.11.2 Character set representations' and 'D.11.3 Programming to use alphanumeric and national character data'. Both are present in the transcription verbatim, with the correct clause number, the correct title, and a correct anchor: '' / '## D.11.2 Character set representations' (:44342) and '' / '## D.11.3 Programming to use alphanumeric and national character data' (:44356). Every body paragraph on the page and both em-dash bullets ('a single character set logically viewed as separate alphanumeric and national coded character sets, or' / 'two separate coded character sets, one alphanumeric and one national') are also present and correct. Not one character of page content is absent. This is a 'missing-heading' finding with no missing heading. (2) THE CLAIM MISDESCRIBES THE PDF, which is the decisive point. The claim asserts the PDF prints each heading 'at the clause depth its number implies, and at the same visual depth as its own first sibling'. I looked at the printed glyphs. On p1102 'D.11 Character sets' and 'D.11.1 General' are typographically IDENTICAL - same bold serif face, same point size, same flush-left indent at the body-text margin, same leading - and on p1103 'D.11.2' and 'D.11.3' are set in that same identical style. The ISO PDF encodes NO visual level distinction whatever among D.11, D.11.1 and D.11.2; the sole hierarchy channel in the printed page is the dotted clause NUMBER itself. That number is transcribed exactly. So there is no typographic feature of the PDF that the markdown fails to reproduce, and the claim's own test ('same visual depth as its own first sibling') is satisfied by '##' precisely as well as by '###', because D.11 and D.11.1 have the same visual depth as each other in the source. Markdown '#' count is an editorial overlay invented by the transcriber, not a transcription of anything on the page - so a wrong '#' count cannot be a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. Meaning is fully preserved: the clause hierarchy is unambiguously recoverable from 'D.11.2', exactly as a reader recovers it from the PDF. (3) THE ASSERTED FILE-WIDE PATTERN IS FACTUALLY FALSE. The claim's mechanism - 'only the FIRST subclause under a parent keeps its correct level and every later sibling is promoted to ##' - does not survive a sweep of Annex D headings. Counterexamples: '#### D.2.3.2.1 General' (:41598) AND '#### D.2.3.2.2 Sequential access mode' (:41607) BOTH retain depth before '## D.2.3.2.3' (:41628); all four of '### D.3.6.1 EXAMPLE 1' through '### D.3.6.4 EXAMPLE 4' (:42639-42716) retain depth; and most damagingly '## D.19.3.3' (:45695) is flattened while its LATER siblings '### D.19.3.4 Object references' (:45731) and '### D.19.3.5 Factory objects' (:45754) are not. The heading levels are not a systematically-broken hierarchy but undirected extraction noise that also hits the top level ('### D.1', '### D.2' vs '## D.3' ... '## D.19'), which means the transcription never purported to encode hierarchy via '#' depth at all - consistent with reading (2). What remains after refutation is a markdown-hygiene/tooling observation, not a fidelity defect, and it belongs in the doc-tooling backlog rather than the spec-reconciliation ledger. Under the standing rule that formatting-only differences that do not change meaning are rejected, and defaulting to false where the finding's stated kind, stated PDF evidence, and stated mechanism are each independently wrong, real=false.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy. Page 1103's two headings (D.11.2 'Character set representations', D.11.3 'Programming to use alphanumeric and national character data') and all of its body text are transcribed completely and verbatim at specs/ISO_COBOL.md:44342 and :44356, each with a correct section anchor. The ISO PDF sets D.11, D.11.1, D.11.2 and D.11.3 in one identical bold heading style at one identical left margin - hierarchy is carried ONLY by the dotted clause number, which the transcription reproduces exactly - so the markdown '#' count is an editorial overlay with no counterpart in the source and cannot diverge from it. Residual (cosmetic, doc-tooling backlog, NOT a reconciliation item): Annex D heading levels in ISO_COBOL.md are internally inconsistent, so any consumer that derives an outline from '#' depth instead of from the clause number will mis-parent clauses. The mechanism named in the claim is also wrong: it is not 'only the first subclause keeps its level' - D.2.3.2.1 and D.2.3.2.2 both keep depth, D.3.6.1 through D.3.6.4 all keep depth, and D.19.3.4/.5 keep depth after D.19.3.3 was flattened - and the noise reaches the top level too (### D.1, ### D.2 vs ## D.3 onward). The correct remedy is a mechanical re-levelling pass that sets every heading's '#' count from its clause number, applied file-wide.
